extracted.subtask_description: A practical how-to guide for creating and writing sitcoms, covering genre conventions, episode and script structure, character work, humor styles, format choices, marketability, and pitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the sitcom genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Know the structure, length, and format to set your show apart; sitcoms usually feature laugh-out-loud moments rooted in relatable life situations and maintain a consistent setting where characters repeatedly find themselves in humorous predicaments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent setting (e.g., family home, workplace) to enable recurring scenarios and character-driven humor; study iconic examples to see how they create repeatable comedic situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode structure and length
rubrics_metrics.description: A typical sitcom episode lasts about 22 minutes (excluding commercials) and commonly follows a three-act structure: Setup, Confrontation, Resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design episodes to fit a 22-minute rhythm; ensure the setup introduces the central conflict, the confrontation heightens it into comedic situations, and the resolution delivers a payoff often with ironic humor or a punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use main plot plus subplots (A/B/C stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a main plot (story A) and one or two subplots (stories B and C) so multiple story arcs unfold within an episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance screen time and interweave subplots so they complement or contrast the main story; subplots can provide tonal or emotional variety and keep audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft relatable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop well-rounded characters with unique backstories and quirks so they resonate with audiences and fuel humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground exaggerated traits in reality to enhance relatability; memorable characters come from distinct personalities and credible motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character backstories
rubrics_metrics.description: Create detailed backstories to provide depth and explain motivations and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use backstories to inform recurring jokes, contradictions, and character growth (example: Del Boy’s larger-than-life persona); avoid one-note characterization by showing why quirks exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character quirks and distinctive voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Give characters specific quirks, speech patterns, or habits that make them stand out and generate humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quirks should be integral to identity and interactions (example: Sheldon Cooper’s fastidiousness); ensure each principal has a voice unique enough to be identifiable in dialogue alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character dynamics and chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Write relationships, chemistry, and interpersonal dynamics that drive comedic situations and recurring arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose settings that promote interaction (e.g., office, coffee shop); foster recurring relational patterns so familiar tensions can be mined each episode (example: camaraderie in Parks and Recreation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor style and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which comedic elements to use—witty dialogue, physical comedy, situational irony, absurdity—and how to blend them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study shows that mix styles effectively (e.g., The Office and Brooklyn Nine-Nine); pick a consistent tone so the audience knows what kind of humor to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setups and punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct effective setups that lay groundwork for jokes and deliver punchlines with proper timing and payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft setups early in the episode or scene and pay them off later; timing and audience expectation are crucial for comedic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and resolution per episode
rubrics_metrics.description: Each episode should present a conflict that is humorously resolved by the end—often with a lesson or ironic twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure stakes are clear enough to create tension but flexible enough to restore the status quo; resolutions should feel earned and comedic rather than arbitrary (example: misunderstandings in The Office).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose single-cam vs. multi-cam format
rubrics_metrics.description: Select single-cam or multi-cam based on production style, pacing, and narrative goals: single-cam allows cinematic control and character depth; multi-cam is faster, cheaper, and driven by dialogue and audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-cam suits complex themes and varied locations (The Office, Arrested Development); multi-cam favors ensemble dynamics and dialogue-driven humor (Friends, The Big Bang Theory). Consider pacing, budget, and intended comedic style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and own a comedic niche
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a niche (workplace, family, buddy, etc.) that fits your interests and strengths to make the show distinctive and attract an audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research successful shows in your chosen niche to identify unique elements worth emulating or subverting; ground your premise in authentic experience for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: identify unique elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your concept stand out by choosing a distinctive setting, putting twists on common tropes, or creating uniquely drawn characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for underused settings (example: The Good Place's afterlife premise) or mashups (Brooklyn Nine-Nine mixing police procedural with comedy) to give familiar formats a fresh spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketability and audience understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand your target demographic and what they find relatable and funny to shape content that appeals to viewers and buyers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research audience preferences and comparable shows (example: The Big Bang Theory’s appeal to geek culture); tailor tone, references, and character dynamics to that audience without sacrificing originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a memorable pitch and logline
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a concise logline that communicates the unique premise and comedic potential; prepare a pitch document with character descriptions, pilot synopsis, and future episode ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice delivering the pitch confidently and succinctly; include the show’s hook, tone, and why it will attract viewers/buyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you know and be authentic
rubrics_metrics.description: Infuse scripts with personal experiences and realistic settings to lend authenticity and relatability to the humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your own life as raw material (example: Larry David’s Curb Your Enthusiasm); authenticity helps ground heightened comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened reality and exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Amplify everyday situations to absurd or heightened levels while maintaining a kernel of truth to maximize comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take relatable premises and push them just far enough to reveal humor without breaking believability (example: Seinfeld’s focus on mundane detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue: natural voice and brisk pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Write dialogue that sounds natural and reflects each character’s voice while maintaining the brisk pace typical of sitcoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnatural exposition; study rapid-fire dialogue examples (e.g., Gilmore Girls for speed) and ensure each character’s speech patterns are distinct and consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-standard formatting and strong opening pages
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow industry-standard script formatting (character headings, scene descriptions) and make the first few pages compelling to hook readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools like Final Draft for proper formatting; ensure opening scenes establish premise, characters, and comedic tone quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise: seek feedback and professional script analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: After drafting, solicit feedback and refine the script using notes from peers or professional script analysis services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterate on drafts, incorporate constructive criticism, and consider paid script analysis for a thorough, industry-aware review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask critical questions during writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously question character motivations, plot strength, subplot integration, setting authenticity, and thematic consistency to ensure depth and realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a checklist of questions (e.g., what motivates this character? does each episode have a strong conflict and resolution? does the subplot tie into the main plot?) to evaluate drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defy genre conventions and subvert tropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally subvert clichés, introduce unexpected plot twists, and create surprising character reactions to stand out and keep audiences engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parody, inversion, or surprising decisions (example: Community’s trope-subversion) and ensure characters can evolve over time to add long-term depth (example: BoJack Horseman).
